module.title: Unit 8: Science Counts: Modals of Ability & Obligation
module.objective: Mampu berbicara tentang kebiasaan masa lalu, menggunakan 'used to', second conditional (I wish), serta memahami perbedaan past simple vs. past continuous dalam konteks penemuan ilmiah dan kehidupan sehari-hari

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Scientific Discoveries and Past Lives
subModules.theme: Science Counts: Modals of Ability, Obligation, and Past Habits
subModules.grammarFocus: Used to, Past Simple vs Past Continuous, and Second Conditional
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Scientific nouns, verbs, and laboratory terms

content.summary: Welcome to Unit 8! In this reading module, you will explore how great scientists worked in the past, how they used to conduct experiments, and how different grammar structures help us talk about past habits, discoveries, and hypothetical situations.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Used to for past habits, Past Simple versus Past Continuous, and Second Conditional sentences.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Terms related to science, inventions, laboratories, and medical research.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the text for general meaning and scanning for specific details like dates, names, and scientific methods.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of short B1 informational texts about science and history.
Locate specific details regarding scientific experiments and past discoveries.
Recognize and apply grammar patterns involving past habits and imaginary scenarios.

contextWarmup.prompt: When you read about famous scientists from the past, what do you usually find most interesting?
options: Learning about the difficult experiments they performed in simple laboratories
Memorizing the exact dates when every scientific book was published
Reading about modern computer games and smartphone applications
contextWarmup.explanation: Option A is correct because the module focuses on how scientists conducted experiments and made discoveries in past centuries.

rules: Use 'used to + verb' to describe habits or states in the past that are no longer true today.
Use the Past Simple for finished actions in the past, and the Past Continuous for actions that were in progress at a specific moment.
Use the Second Conditional ('if' + past simple, 'would' + verb) to talk about unreal or hypothetical situations in the present or future.

commonTrap.explanation: Students often confuse 'used to' with 'be used to'. Remember that 'used to' describes past habits, while 'be used to' means to be familiar with something.
commonTrap.wrong: He is use to work in a laboratory.
commonTrap.correct: He used to work in a laboratory when he was younger.

paragraphs: Long before modern technology existed, people used to wonder why things happened around them. Ancient scientists did not have computers or advanced laboratories, but they used their eyes and simple tools to observe nature. For example, Isaac Newton was sitting under a tree when an apple fell to the ground. While he was watching the apple, he started thinking about gravity.

In later centuries, inventors created remarkable machines that changed human life forever. Louis Pasteur worked hard in his laboratory to prevent dangerous diseases from spreading. If scientists did not conduct such important experiments every day, modern medicine would not be as advanced as it is today. Every great discovery helps humanity move forward.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Science Counts and Past Habits

content.summary: Focus on listening for past habits using 'used to' and conditional wishes about technology and science history. Pay attention to how speakers stress auxiliary verbs and link words in casual conversation.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about past habits and technology
Identify details such as specific entertainment activities and personal wishes
Notice how words link together in connected speech during fast dialogue

keyPhrases.phrase: What did they use to do
keyPhrases.note: Used to ask about past routines and habits that no longer happen.
Used to express an unreal wish about the present moment.
Common collocation when discussing modern technology dependence.
Refers to a specific period in the past.

connectedSpeech.note: The auxiliary 'did' and pronoun 'you' merge into a single softer sound in rapid speech.
The infinitive marker 'to' reduces to a schwa sound before a consonant.
The final /d/ in read drops slightly before the plosive /b/ sound.
The verb 'was' weakens to a schwa sound in casual conversational pacing.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Science Counts and Past Habits

content.summary: Practical guide on writing about past habits, scientific discoveries, and hypothetical situations using modals of ability and obligation.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Expressing Past Habits with Used To
blueprintItems.example: Scientists used to believe the Earth was the center of the universe.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Combining Past Simple and Past Continuous
blueprintItems.formula: While + subject + past continuous, subject + past simple
blueprintItems.example: While Newton was sitting in his garden, an apple fell from the tree.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Writing Hypothetical Situations
blueprintItems.formula: If + past simple, subject + would + base verb
blueprintItems.example: If we had better laboratory equipment, we would finish the experiment today.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always spell 'used to' without the final 'd' in negative sentences and questions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Researchers didn't used to measure gravity this way.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Researchers didn't use to measure gravity this way.
mechanicsRules.why: The auxiliary verb 'did' already carries the past tense marker, so the main verb takes its base form.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after dependent time clauses beginning with 'While' or 'When'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: While Marie Curie was studying uranium she discovered polonium.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: While Marie Curie was studying uranium, she discovered polonium.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates the introductory dependent clause from the main independent clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize scientific names of principles or laws only when they include proper nouns.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Newton's first law of motion and ohm's law are important.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Newton's first law of motion and Ohm's law are important.
mechanicsRules.why: Names derived from specific scientists are proper nouns and require capitalization.

sampleSentences.en: Ancient astronomers used to map the stars using simple wooden tools.
sampleSentences.id: Astronomer kuno dulu memetakan bintang-bintang menggunakan alat kayu sederhana.

sampleSentences.en: While the chemist was mixing the liquids, the color changed rapidly.
sampleSentences.id: Saat ahli kimia sedang mencampurkan cairan-cairan itu, warnanya berubah dengan cepat.

sampleSentences.en: If I were a famous inventor, I would create a clean energy source.
sampleSentences.id: Jika saya adalah seorang penemu terkenal, saya akan menciptakan sumber energi bersih.

sampleSentences.en: I wish we had more time to complete this science project.
sampleSentences.id: Saya berharap kita punya lebih banyak waktu untuk menyelesaikan proyek sains ini.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Capitalize the first word of the sentence and use proper apostrophe in 'didn't'.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Capitalize proper names and place a comma after the introductory dependent clause.

mechanicsChallenges.translation: Jika Thomas Edison gagal, ia akan mencoba lagi.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use a comma after the 'if' clause in second conditional sentences.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Describe Past Scientific Habits
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences about how students used to learn science before modern technology. Use 'used to' and 'didn't use to'.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Students used to read heavy textbooks in the library. They didn't use to watch video simulations on computers. Teachers used to write notes on large blackboards.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Write your sentences about past learning methods here...

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: A Hypothetical Scientific Discovery
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences using the second conditional about what you would do if you were a famous scientist.
guidedLabChallenges.example: If I were a famous scientist, I would invent a machine to clean the oceans. If everyone used clean energy, cities would have fresh air. I wish I could travel to Mars one day.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the affirmative sentence into the negative form using 'used to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: People used to believe the earth was flat.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'didn't use to' instead of 'used to'.
targetAnswers: People didn't use to believe the earth was flat.
People did not use to believe the earth was flat.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To make 'used to' negative in the past, use 'didn't use to' followed by the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using 'While':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Alexander Fleming was examining bacteria. A mold grew in the petri dish.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'While Alexander Fleming was examining bacteria...'
targetAnswers: While Alexander Fleming was examining bacteria, a mold grew in the petri dish.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past continuous for the longer background action and past simple for the shorter interrupting action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix all capitalization and punctuation errors in the following sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: while marie curie was working in her laboratory she discovered radium.
practicumQuestions.hint: Check the capitalization of the name and the comma placement.
targetAnswers: While Marie Curie was working in her laboratory, she discovered radium.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns like 'Marie Curie' must be capitalized, and a comma is required after the introductory 'While' clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the second conditional sentence with the correct form of the verb in parentheses:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If we (have) microscopes in every classroom, students would learn biology faster.
practicumQuestions.hint: The past simple form of 'have' is required in the if-clause.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The second conditional structure uses 'If + past simple' (had) in the condition clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this sentence into a question using 'used to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: You used to study chemistry at university.
targetAnswers: Did you use to study chemistry at university?
Did you use to study chemistry at university
practicumQuestions.explanation: Questions in the past with 'used to' begin with 'Did' and use 'use to' without the 'd'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence using the correct modal verb of ability in the past:
practicumQuestions.promptText: When Albert Einstein was young, he (be able to / can) solve complex math problems easily.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the past form of ability for a general skill in the past.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Both 'could' and 'was able to' express past ability.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Identify and correct the mistake regarding 'used to' in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Scientists didnt use to have digital instruments.
practicumQuestions.hint: Look closely at the auxiliary negative form 'didnt'.
targetAnswers: Scientists didn't use to have digital instruments.
Scientists did not use to have digital instruments.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The contraction 'didn't' requires an apostrophe between the 'n' and the 't'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'wish' to express a present regret or desire:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I don't know enough about astronomy.
targetAnswers: I wish I knew more about astronomy.
I wish I knew enough about astronomy.
practicumQuestions.explanation: After 'I wish', we use the past simple tense to talk about present wishes that are contrary to fact.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the second conditional consequence clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If Isaac Newton didn't notice the apple, he (not / formulate) the law of universal gravitation in that exact way.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'wouldn't' followed by the base verb.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The second conditional result clause requires 'would' + base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'used to' in the affirmative form:
practicumQuestions.promptText: In the past, doctors prescribed different treatments for common illnesses.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace the time phrase with 'Doctors used to...'
targetAnswers: Doctors used to prescribe different treatments for common illnesses.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Used to' expresses repeated past actions or states that no longer happen or exist.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Science Counts: Modals of Ability & Obligation

content.summary: Master the pronunciation of key scientific terms and modals of ability and obligation in spoken English. Clear articulation helps listeners understand complex ideas during presentations and discussions.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on pronouncing modal verbs with weak forms in connected speech. Words like 'can', 'must', and 'should' often lose their full vowel sound unless they are emphasized for importance.

pillars.name: Modal Weak Forms
pillars.explanation: In fast spoken English, auxiliary and modal verbs are often reduced. For example, 'must' sounds like 'mus' before consonant sounds.

pillars.name: Scientific Vocabulary Stress
pillars.target: Accurate syllable stress in multi-syllable nouns
pillars.explanation: Words ending in -ion, -ist, and -y have fixed stress patterns. For example, 'experiment' stresses the second syllable, while 'laboratory' stresses the first.

pillars.name: Sentence Chunking
pillars.target: Pause naturally at logical phrase boundaries
pillars.explanation: Group related words together when talking about scientific experiments and obligations so your speech sounds natural and easy to follow.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Both nouns have stress on the second syllable, ending in an unstressed suffix.
Both terms place the primary stress on the very first syllable.
Notice how the stress shifts from the second syllable noun to the final syllable verb.
Both terms feature strong root syllables with clear vowel sounds.

drills.hint: Pronounce 'can' as /kən/ unless you want to emphasize ability.

drills.hint: Pause slightly after 'cure' before saying the purpose clause.

What safety rules you had to follow in the laboratory
What scientific discovery or result you achieved

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond to your lab partner regarding science rules and safety equipment.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Partner: Do you think we are allowed to eat snacks inside the school laboratory?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are discussing safety regulations with your lab partner before starting a biology project.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: No, we must not eat inside the laboratory because it violates safety rules.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use modals of obligation like 'must not' correctly in conversational dialogue.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Discuss experiment preparations with your classmate.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Partner: Can you finish writing the research report by tonight?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your classmate is stressed about finishing a science project deadline.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, I have to finish the report tonight so we can submit it tomorrow.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Respond naturally using 'have to' for external obligation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Talk about past scientific requirements with your teacher.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Teacher: Did scientists have special equipment during early medical research?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are chatting with your history of science teacher after class.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, early scientists had to build their own tools to make new discoveries.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use the past obligation form 'had to' to discuss historical scientific contexts.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Plan a science fair presentation with your partner.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Partner: Should we present our invention or our experiment results first?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are organizing the structure of your upcoming science fair presentation.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We should present our experiment results before showing the final invention.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'should' to offer polite advice and suggestions in collaborative planning.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the target sentence aloud, focusing on accurate vocabulary pronunciation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence: A brilliant scientist made a remarkable discovery in the physics laboratory.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: A brilliant scientist made a remarkable discovery in the physics laboratory.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Pronounce scientific vocabulary with correct syllable stress and clear vowel articulation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the target sentence aloud, paying attention to modal verb structures.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence: Students must follow every safety instruction when conducting experiments.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Students must follow every safety instruction when conducting experiments.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Emphasize modal verbs of obligation clearly within the sentence structure.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the sentence aloud, making sure to hit the correct syllable stress on multi-syllable scientific terms.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence: The new medical invention will help doctors cure the dangerous disease.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The new medical invention will help doctors cure the dangerous disease.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Maintain primary stress on the correct syllable of words like 'invention' and 'medical'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the question aloud using correct rising intonation for yes-no questions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this question with natural rising intonation: Can we use this laboratory equipment without permission?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Can we use this laboratory equipment without permission?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use rising pitch at the end of modal questions to indicate inquiry and engagement.
